questions.stem: The charge nurse is observing a new graduate nurse care for a client admitted with Clostridioides difficile infection who has had six liquid stools today. Which action by the new nurse requires the charge nurse to intervene?

options.text: Puts on a gown and gloves before entering the room to drop off the meal tray
Wipes the shared glucometer with a bleach-based wipe before taking it out
Uses alcohol hand rub after taking off the gloves and leaving the room
Leaves the disposable stethoscope in the room when the shift is over

rationale.correct: C. difficile forms spores that resist alcohol, so hand hygiene after care is soap and water. Equipment that leaves the room is cleaned with a sporicidal agent.

perOption.a: Contact precautions call for a gown and gloves on entering the room, even when the nurse does not plan to touch the client.
perOption.b: A sporicidal (bleach-based) product is the right disinfectant for equipment that must leave a C. difficile room.
perOption.c: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores; handwashing with soap and water removes them mechanically.
perOption.d: Dedicated equipment stays in the room so spores are not carried to other clients.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Use soap and water, not alcohol rub, after caring for a client with C. difficile.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old client who recently moved from a country with a high rate of tuberculosis is admitted with a 6-week cough, night sweats, weight loss and a cavity in the right upper lobe on the chest x-ray. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Admit the client to an airborne infection isolation room with negative pressure
Wear a fit-tested N95 respirator for every entry, including brief ones
Place a surgical mask on the client when the client leaves the room for tests
Collect three sputum specimens for acid-fast bacilli, including early morning ones
Have the client wear an N95 respirator when transported for the CT scan
End airborne isolation once the first sputum smear comes back negative

rationale.correct: Suspected active TB needs airborne precautions: a negative-pressure room, an N95 for staff, a surgical mask on the client outside the room, and three negative sputum smears before isolation ends.

perOption.a: Negative pressure keeps droplet nuclei from leaving the room.
perOption.b: Droplet nuclei stay in the air, so the respirator is needed whenever anyone enters.
perOption.c: A surgical mask on the client traps the large particles the client coughs out; a respirator on the client is not needed.
perOption.d: Three specimens 8 to 24 hours apart, with at least one early morning sample, are needed to diagnose TB and later to end isolation.
perOption.e: Respirators protect the wearer from inhaling particles; the client wears a surgical mask to contain secretions.
perOption.f: Isolation continues until three sputum smears are negative and the client is improving on treatment.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply airborne precautions for suspected tuberculosis.

questions.stem: The nurse on an admission unit is placing four new clients. Each will have a private room. Which client requires droplet precautions in addition to standard precautions?

options.text: A client with disseminated herpes zoster who has lesions on the trunk and both legs
A client with suspected meningococcal meningitis who received the first antibiotic dose
A client with norovirus who is having frequent vomiting and loose stools
A client with a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection of a leg wound

rationale.correct: Droplet precautions (surgical mask within about 2 m, private room) cover meningococcal disease, pertussis, influenza, mumps and rubella. Disseminated zoster is airborne plus contact.

perOption.a: Disseminated zoster needs airborne and contact precautions, like varicella, not droplet.
perOption.b: Neisseria meningitidis spreads by large droplets; droplet precautions continue for 24 hours of effective therapy.
perOption.c: Norovirus spreads by contact with stool, vomit and surfaces, so contact precautions are used.
perOption.d: MRSA in a wound spreads by contact.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify infections that need droplet precautions.

questions.stem: The infection prevention nurse is reviewing isolation signs on a medical unit. For each condition, choose the transmission-based precautions the client needs in addition to standard precautions.

rows.text: Meningococcal meningitis, first 24 hours of antibiotics

rationale.correct: Airborne: measles, varicella, disseminated zoster, TB. Droplet: meningococcus, pertussis, influenza, mumps, rubella. Contact: C. difficile, MRSA, VRE, scabies, lice.

perOption.r1:c1: Measles virus stays suspended in the air and needs airborne precautions.
perOption.r1:c2: A surgical mask does not filter the airborne measles virus.
perOption.r1:c3: Contact precautions alone do not stop airborne spread.
perOption.r2:c2: N. meningitidis spreads by large respiratory droplets.
perOption.r2:c3: Contact is not the main route.
perOption.r3:c1: C. difficile is not spread through the air.
perOption.r3:c2: C. difficile is not spread by respiratory droplets.
perOption.r3:c3: Spores spread on hands and surfaces, so contact precautions are needed.
perOption.r4:c3: Contact precautions alone are not enough.
perOption.r5:c1: TB spreads through airborne droplet nuclei.
perOption.r5:c2: A surgical mask and droplet precautions do not filter TB particles.
perOption.r5:c3: TB is not spread by contact.
perOption.r6:c2: VRE is not spread by droplets.
perOption.r6:c3: VRE spreads on hands, equipment and surfaces.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Match common infections to their transmission-based precautions.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to enter the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions. Place the steps for putting on personal protective equipment in order.

items.text: Put on gloves, pulling the cuffs over the gown sleeves
Put on goggles or a face shield

rationale.correct: CDC order for putting on PPE: hand hygiene, gown, mask or respirator, eye protection, gloves.

perOption.a: Clean hands come first so the PPE is not contaminated.
perOption.b: The gown goes on first so the mask ties and gloves can go over it.
perOption.c: The mask is placed before eye protection so the face shield or goggles fit over it.
perOption.d: Eye protection goes over the mask.
perOption.e: Gloves go on last and cover the gown cuffs to protect the wrists.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Put on personal protective equipment in the correct sequence.

questions.stem: The nurse is leaving the room of a client on droplet and contact precautions after suctioning the client. The nurse is wearing a gown, gloves, goggles and a surgical mask. Which item should the nurse remove last, just before performing hand hygiene?

options.text: Gloves
Goggles
Gown
Mask

rationale.correct: Removal order: gloves, goggles or face shield, gown, then mask or respirator, then hand hygiene. The most contaminated items come off first.

perOption.a: Gloves are the most contaminated item and come off first.
perOption.b: Eye protection comes off after the gloves, handled by the headband or earpieces.
perOption.c: The gown comes off after the goggles (or together with the gloves), before the mask.
perOption.d: The mask comes off last, by the ties or ear loops without touching the front, followed by hand hygiene.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Remove personal protective equipment in the correct sequence.

questions.stem: The nurse is observing a nursing student set up a sterile field on an overbed table for a central line dressing change. Which action by the student requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Pours sterile saline into a sterile cup from a few inches above it, without touching the cup
Keeps sterile items 2.5 cm (1 inch) inside the drape's edge
Goes on with the setup after saline soaked through the drape onto the table
Holds the saline bottle with the label in the palm and discards a small amount first

rationale.correct: A sterile field that becomes wet is contaminated by strike-through and must be set up again. Items stay inside the 2.5 cm border and the field stays in view.

perOption.a: Pouring from a short height without contact keeps the cup sterile; splashing is the risk, not the height itself.
perOption.b: The outer 2.5 cm border is considered unsterile, so items are placed inside it.
perOption.c: A wet sterile field is contaminated because moisture wicks microorganisms up from the unsterile surface beneath (strike-through).
perOption.d: Protecting the label and pouring off a little saline to clean the lip are correct technique.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize breaks in surgical asepsis.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client with a history of falls is admitted with heart failure and receives furosemide 40 mg IV twice a day. The client gets up at night to urinate and is sometimes confused on waking. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the bed in its lowest position with the wheels locked
Offer help to the toilet on a schedule, including just before sleep
Activate a bed exit alarm when the client is in bed
Ask the provider to move the second furosemide dose to bedtime
Raise all four side rails at night so the client stays in bed
Turn off all room lights at night so the client sleeps more deeply

rationale.correct: Prevent falls with a safe environment and planned help timed around the client's needs, such as diuretic timing and toileting, not with restraint.

perOption.a: A low, locked bed shortens any fall and keeps the bed from rolling as the client gets up.
perOption.b: Scheduled toileting prevents rushed, unassisted trips caused by the diuretic.
perOption.c: An alarm alerts staff as the client starts to get up, so help arrives in time.
perOption.d: A bedtime diuretic increases night-time urination and falls; the second dose is usually given in the mid-afternoon.
perOption.e: Four raised rails count as a restraint and lead to worse injuries when clients climb over them.
perOption.f: A night light lets the client see on waking; darkness raises fall risk.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan interventions to prevent falls in hospitalized clients.

questions.stem: The nurse is supervising assistive personnel (AP) caring for a client in soft wrist restraints prescribed for pulling at an endotracheal tube. Which action by the AP requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Secures each restraint to the part of the bed frame that moves when the head is raised
Removes one restraint at a time every 2 hours to give range of motion and skin care
Ties the restraint strap to the bed frame using a secure square knot
Checks that two fingers fit between the restraint and the client's wrist

rationale.correct: Restraints are tied to the bed frame (not the side rail) with a quick-release knot, checked for circulation and released regularly for care.

perOption.a: Tying to the movable frame is correct, because the restraint then moves with the client instead of pulling.
perOption.b: Releasing one limb at a time allows care while the client stays safe.
perOption.c: A square knot cannot be released quickly in an emergency; restraints are tied with a quick-release knot.
perOption.d: Two fingers' space keeps circulation intact while the restraint stays secure.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply and monitor physical restraints safely.

questions.stem: A confused client on a medical unit keeps pulling at a nasogastric tube. The provider writes, "Soft wrist restraints PRN for agitation." Mitts have not been tried. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Apply the restraints whenever the client is agitated, and document each episode
Try mitts first and use the wrist restraints only if the mitts do not work
Ask the client's spouse for written consent before applying the restraints
Call the provider, because the order must be time-limited and specific

rationale.correct: PRN restraint orders are never valid. The nurse tries less restrictive measures and obtains a specific, time-limited order when restraint is needed.

perOption.a: Restraint orders cannot be written PRN, so acting on this order is not allowed.
perOption.b: Trying the less restrictive measure is right, but the PRN restraint order is still invalid and must be clarified.
perOption.c: Family consent does not replace a valid, time-limited provider order.
perOption.d: Restraint orders must name the reason, type and time limit and be renewed after reassessment; PRN orders are not permitted.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that restraint orders cannot be written PRN.

questions.stem: The nurse needs to use a portable fire extinguisher on a small wastebasket fire. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Sweep the nozzle from side to side
Aim the nozzle at the base of the fire

rationale.correct: PASS: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep. The extinguisher is used only after the RACE steps (rescue, alarm, contain) for a small, contained fire.

perOption.a: The pin locks the handle; it must be removed first.
perOption.b: Aiming at the base puts out the fuel source, not just the flames.
perOption.c: Squeezing the handle releases the extinguishing agent.
perOption.d: A sweeping motion covers the whole base of the fire.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Use a fire extinguisher with the PASS sequence.

questions.stem: The nurse is triaging victims of a bus crash using the START system. Which victim should the nurse tag red (immediate)?

options.text: A victim who walked to the triage area holding a deep forearm laceration that is oozing blood
A victim who cannot walk, breathes 24 times a minute, has a radial pulse, but does not obey commands
A victim who is not breathing and still does not breathe after the airway is repositioned
A victim with a closed femur fracture who follows commands, respirations 22/min, refill under 2 seconds

rationale.correct: START: walking is green; no breathing after airway repositioning is black; respirations over 30, no radial pulse or refill over 2 seconds, or not following commands is red; everyone else is yellow.

perOption.a: Anyone who can walk is tagged green (minor) first, then reassessed.
perOption.b: Breathing under 30/min with a radial pulse passes the first two checks, but failing to follow simple commands meets the immediate criteria.
perOption.c: No breathing after the airway is opened is tagged black (expectant).
perOption.d: Breathing, perfusion and mental status are adequate, so this victim can wait and is tagged yellow (delayed).

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply START triage categories in a mass-casualty event.

questions.stem: An external disaster has been declared and the hospital needs medical-surgical beds for incoming casualties. Which client should the nurse recommend for early discharge?

options.text: A client 2 days after an appendectomy who is walking and eating a regular diet
A client with pneumonia, afebrile for 12 hours, on day 2 of IV antibiotics
A client 1 day after a hip fracture repair who got out of bed for the first time today
A client with heart failure on IV furosemide whose weight is up 1 kg today

rationale.correct: During a disaster, discharge first the stable clients whose recovery is predictable and who no longer need hospital-level treatment.

perOption.a: This client is stable, recovering as expected and can finish recovering at home.
perOption.b: The client is improving but has not yet met criteria to switch to oral antibiotics.
perOption.c: The client still needs inpatient pain control, anticoagulation and mobility progression.
perOption.d: Rising weight on IV diuretics shows the heart failure is not yet controlled.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose clients for early discharge during a disaster.

questions.stem: A client with a sealed cervical radiation implant calls the nurse and says, "Something fell out into the bed." The nurse sees the implant on the sheet. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Pick up the implant with double gloves and place it in the room's biohazard container
Use long-handled forceps to put the implant in the lead container in the room
Put on a lead apron and gently reinsert the implant into the vaginal applicator
Leave the room, close the door and wait there until the radiation safety officer arrives

rationale.correct: Time, distance and shielding protect against radiation. Move a dislodged sealed source with long-handled forceps into the lead container in the room, then notify radiation safety.

perOption.a: Gloves do not block radiation, and a radioactive source never goes in biohazard waste.
perOption.b: Forceps add distance and the lead container adds shielding, both of which limit exposure.
perOption.c: Only the radiation oncology team repositions an implant.
perOption.d: Leaving the source on the bed keeps exposing the client; it is contained first, then the officer is called.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond safely to a dislodged sealed radiation implant.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to hang an IV bag of a cytotoxic chemotherapy drug that the pharmacy has already mixed. Which personal protective equipment should the nurse wear while spiking and hanging the bag?

options.text: One pair of chemotherapy-tested gloves and a cloth cover gown
Two pairs of sterile surgical gloves and a fluid-resistant mask
Two pairs of chemotherapy-tested gloves and an impermeable gown
A single pair of nitrile examination gloves and a face shield

rationale.correct: Cytotoxic drugs are absorbed through skin even after mixing. Wear double chemotherapy-tested gloves and an impermeable gown, plus eye and face protection when splashing is possible.

perOption.a: Cloth gowns absorb hazardous drugs instead of blocking them, and one pair of gloves is not enough.
perOption.b: Sterile gloves are not tested against chemotherapy agents, and a mask does not protect the skin.
perOption.c: Hazardous-drug guidance calls for double chemotherapy-tested gloves and a disposable gown that resists permeation.
perOption.d: Eye protection is added when splashing is likely, but single exam gloves do not give enough protection.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Select PPE for handling hazardous drugs.

questions.stem: The nurse is about to give a scheduled antibiotic and finds that the client's identification band was cut off to start a new IV. The band is on the bedside table. The client is alert and oriented. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the client's name and date of birth, and give the drug because they match the record
Check the name and record number on the band on the table against the medication record
Ask the client's spouse, who is at the bedside, to confirm the client's full name
Hold the dose until a new band is on, then check two identifiers and give it

rationale.correct: Check at least two identifiers, such as name and date of birth, against the band the client is wearing and the medication record. Never use the room number.

perOption.a: Two identifiers are compared with the band on the client, which is missing; the band is replaced first.
perOption.b: A band that is not on the client cannot identify the client.
perOption.c: A visitor is not an approved identifier.
perOption.d: The client must wear an identification band, and two identifiers are matched with it and the medication record before giving the drug.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify clients with two identifiers before care.

questions.stem: At 1130 the nurse realizes that a client with type 2 diabetes was given 10 units of regular insulin at 1100 instead of the prescribed 1 unit. Lunch trays arrive at 1215. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Review the label on the insulin vial to find out how the error happened
Check the client's glucose and look for signs of hypoglycemia
Notify the provider of the error right away
Complete an incident report and notify the nurse manager of the error

rationale.correct: After a medication error, assess the client first, then notify the provider, treat as prescribed, document the facts in the record and complete an incident report.

perOption.a: Finding the cause matters for the incident report, but it does nothing for the client now.
perOption.b: Regular insulin peaks in 2 to 4 hours; assessing for harm comes first after any medication error.
perOption.c: The provider is notified promptly, with the assessment findings in hand.
perOption.d: Reports are required, but only after the client is safe.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a medication error in priority order.

questions.stem: At 0215 the nurse finds a client sitting on the floor beside the bed. The client says, "I was going to the bathroom." The nurse finds no injuries and notifies the provider. Which entry should the nurse write in the medical record?

options.text: "Client fell out of bed because the side rail was down. Incident report completed."
"0215 sitting on floor by bed. States 'I was going to the bathroom.' No injury seen."
"Client fell because of confusion and should have been checked on more often by staff."
"Client found on floor at 0215. See the incident report for details of the fall."

rationale.correct: Chart only what was seen, heard and done. The incident report is a separate quality document and is never mentioned in the chart.

perOption.a: The cause is assumed, and the incident report is never mentioned in the medical record.
perOption.b: This entry is objective, includes the client's own words and the assessment, and leaves out blame.
perOption.c: Opinions and blame do not belong in the medical record.
perOption.d: Referring to the incident report puts it in the record and removes its confidential, quality-improvement status.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Document an adverse event objectively.

questions.stem: The nurse notices that the power cord of a client's IV infusion pump is frayed near the plug. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wrap the frayed area with electrical tape and keep using the pump
Replace the pump, tag the damaged one and send it for repair
Finish this infusion, then report the cord
Unplug the pump and run the infusion on its battery until it is fixed

rationale.correct: Remove damaged electrical equipment from use at once, label it and report it so no one else uses it.

perOption.a: Tape does not make a damaged cord safe; it is still a shock and fire hazard.
perOption.b: Faulty equipment is taken out of service, labeled and sent to biomedical engineering.
perOption.c: Continued use risks shock or fire.
perOption.d: The pump still needs inspection, and the battery will run out.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Remove unsafe equipment from service.

questions.stem: The home health nurse documents a first visit with an 82-year-old client with macular degeneration who lives alone and takes warfarin. Highlight the findings that are safety hazards.

segments.text: Throw rugs are placed in the hallway and kitchen
A space heater sits 30 cm (1 ft) from the bedroom curtains
Grab bars are installed beside the toilet and in the shower
Pills are kept in unlabeled containers on the counter
Medications for the week are set out in a pill organizer by a daughter
The stairway light switch is only at the bottom of the stairs

rationale.correct: A home safety assessment looks for fall hazards (rugs, poor lighting), fire hazards (space heaters) and medication risks, and recognises protective measures already in place.

perOption.s2: Loose rugs are a leading cause of tripping and falls in older adults.
perOption.s4: Space heaters need about 1 m (3 ft) of clearance from anything flammable.
perOption.s6: Grab bars reduce bathroom falls; they are protective.
perOption.s8: Unlabeled medications raise the risk of taking the wrong drug or dose, which is dangerous with warfarin.
perOption.s10: A filled pill organizer helps a client with low vision take the right doses.
perOption.s12: Coming down dark stairs raises fall risk; switches are needed at both ends.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize hazards during a home safety assessment.

questions.stem: The nurse has taught a client with COPD about using oxygen at home. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll keep my oxygen at least 10 feet from the gas stove and the fireplace."
"I'll keep the spare cylinders upright in their stand in a cool room."
"I'll put petroleum jelly on my nose and lips when they get dry."
"I'll post no-smoking signs on my doors."

rationale.correct: Oxygen feeds fire: keep it away from flames and heat, store cylinders upright, allow no smoking, and use water-based, not petroleum-based, products.

perOption.a: Keeping oxygen well away from flames and heat is correct.
perOption.b: Securing cylinders upright away from heat prevents falls and valve damage.
perOption.c: Petroleum products are flammable in an oxygen-rich setting; water-based lubricant is used instead.
perOption.d: No-smoking signs and rules are correct.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate teaching on home oxygen safety.

questions.stem: A client with a seizure disorder is sitting in a chair in the room when the client stiffens and begins rhythmic jerking of all four limbs. The client has a prescription for IV lorazepam for seizures lasting more than 5 minutes. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Note the time the seizure started so its length can be reported
Ease the client to the floor and turn the client onto one side
Insert an oral airway between the teeth to protect the client's airway
Prepare the IV lorazepam so it is ready at the 5-minute mark

rationale.correct: During a tonic-clonic seizure, protect the client from injury and keep the airway clear first; then time the seizure and give rescue medication if it lasts 5 minutes.

perOption.a: Timing matters for the lorazepam decision, but it comes after protecting the client from a fall.
perOption.b: Lowering the client prevents injury from a fall, and the side-lying position keeps the airway clear.
perOption.c: Nothing is placed in the mouth during a seizure; it can break teeth or block the airway.
perOption.d: The nurse stays with the client and calls for help; the drug is given only if the seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Protect a client during a tonic-clonic seizure.

questions.stem: The nurse is observing assistive personnel move and position clients on a medical unit. Which action by the AP requires the nurse to intervene?

options.text: Raises the bed to waist height before giving a bed bath
Moves a heavy client up in bed alone by pulling under the arms
Uses a mechanical lift for a client who cannot bear weight
Stands with the feet apart and the knees bent before lifting

rationale.correct: Safe handling: use friction-reducing devices, lifts and enough staff; never pull a client under the arms.

perOption.a: Working at waist height reduces back strain.
perOption.b: Pulling under the arms can dislocate the shoulder and tear the skin; use a friction-reducing sheet and two staff.
perOption.c: A lift is the safe way to transfer a client who cannot bear weight.
perOption.d: A wide base and bent knees protect the back.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize unsafe client handling.

questions.stem: A person wearing scrubs and no hospital badge enters a postpartum room and says, "I need to take the baby to the nursery for a hearing test." The mother looks at the nurse. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Let the person take the newborn, because a hearing test is due before discharge
Keep the newborn with the mother and call security to verify the person
Walk with the person and the newborn to the nursery to watch the test
Ask the mother whether she is comfortable letting the person take the newborn

rationale.correct: Only staff wearing the unit's special identification transport infants. Anyone else is challenged, the infant stays with the parent, and security is called.

perOption.a: The test is real, but anyone without the unit's identification must not take an infant.
perOption.b: Staff without proper identification must not handle the infant; the nurse protects the newborn and starts the security plan.
perOption.c: Going along does not confirm identity and still lets an unknown person handle the infant.
perOption.d: The mother cannot verify staff identity; the facility's security plan applies.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply infant security measures.

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia has an absolute neutrophil count of 400/mm3 and a temperature of 37.4 °C (99.3 °F). The client's partner wants to bring flowers and the client's 6-year-old, who has a runny nose. Select the 3 actions the nurse should take.

options.text: Perform hand hygiene every time before entering the room
Ask that fresh flowers and plants be kept out of the room
Avoid rectal temperatures, suppositories and enemas
Let the child visit if the child wears a surgical mask
Wear an N95 respirator whenever entering the room
Move the client to a negative-pressure isolation room

rationale.correct: An ANC under 500/mm3 is severe neutropenia. Protective precautions keep pathogens away from the client: hand hygiene, no plants or ill visitors, and no rectal procedures.

perOption.a: Hand hygiene is the most effective way to prevent infection in a neutropenic client.
perOption.b: Flowers, plants and their water can carry bacteria and fungi.
perOption.c: Rectal procedures can injure the mucosa and let bacteria into the blood.
perOption.d: Anyone with signs of infection should not visit a client with severe neutropenia.
perOption.e: Respirators protect staff from airborne infections; they are not part of neutropenic precautions.
perOption.f: Negative pressure is for airborne infections; protective environments use positive pressure.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
